texts: bad: 'in autumn and early winter' packs two seasons into one generic clause, and the translator hid them behind an opaque 'or' head, so neither season is retrievable afterwards; 'early winter' also has no encodable time form, so 'early' becomes an invented symbol. Carry each season in the storm's own label, one sentence per season: 'Autumn storms come over the Cold Sea. Early-winter storms come over the Cold Sea.' That yields two clean per-storm rules with the season kept inside the kind word, and it matches the way 'Autumn storms ...' already parses further down this section.
good. both compounds keep their head genus, the equinox is the doer of a begin event on the storm season, and the bare present correctly gets no tense marking.
good. parses as a fireable per-storm rule, with 'sometimes' both lowering the strength and being recorded as the quantifier word, and Cliff Path kept as a name with the lanterns linked to it.
good. the 'in winter' modifier licenses a reified staying state, the fleet stays one participant rather than being split into member-by-member claims, and the harbor position rides that state.

mixed: everything emitted is right, but 'far' has no slot available on an event, so it is dropped and the parse says only that the fleet sails in summer -- the distance, which is the point of the sentence, is lost. Hang the distance on a destination so it survives: 'The fleet sails to distant waters in summer.'
good. the safe return is reified with no tense, so it is recorded as what the depending is about rather than asserted to have happened, and 'depends on' puts the lanterns in its own on-slot.
good. 'bad for lanterns' and 'bad for fishing' each become one property with its argument recorded, and the sentence lands as a fireable rule leading from the first to the second.
